title: No. 37 — Concerning the Difficulties of the Convention in Devising a Proper Form of Government. (Madison)
paragraphs: In reviewing the defects of the existing Confederation, and showing that they cannot be remedied by a government of less energy than the one now proposed, several of its most important principles have come up for consideration. But since the ultimate aim of these papers is to determine clearly and fully the merits of this Constitution, and the wisdom of adopting it, our plan cannot be complete without a more critical and thorough survey of the convention's work. We must examine it on all sides, compare it in all its parts, and calculate its probable effects. To carry out this remaining task with the impressions needed for a just and fair conclusion, some reflections must be indulged here, which candor naturally suggests.

It is a misfortune inseparable from human affairs that public measures are rarely investigated with that spirit of moderation essential to a just estimate of their real tendency to advance or obstruct the public good. This spirit is more often diminished than promoted by occasions that demand its unusual exercise. To those who have learned by experience to attend to this consideration, it could not be surprising that the convention's act, which recommends so many important changes and innovations, which can be viewed in so many lights, and which touches the springs of so many passions and interests, should find or excite dispositions on both sides unfriendly to fair discussion and accurate judgment of its merits. Some, by their own publications, have made it too obvious that they have scanned the proposed Constitution not only with a predisposition to censure but with a predetermined intent to condemn. The language of others betrays an opposite predetermination or bias, which must render their opinions also of little weight. In placing these different characters on a level regarding the weight of their opinions, I do not insinuate that there may not be a material difference in the purity of their intentions. It is just to remark in favor of the latter that, since our situation is universally admitted to be peculiarly critical and to require that something be done for our relief, the predetermined supporter of what has been done may have been swayed by these considerations as well as by sinister ones. The predetermined adversary, on the other hand, can have been governed by no excusable motive whatever. The intentions of the first may be upright, though they may also be culpable. The views of the second cannot be upright and must be culpable. But the truth is, these papers are not addressed to people of either character. They appeal only to those who, along with sincere zeal for their country's happiness, possess a temper favorable to a just estimate of the means of promoting it.

People of this character will examine the convention's plan, not with a disposition to find or magnify faults, but recognizing that a faultless plan was not to be expected. They will not merely make allowance for errors caused by the fallibility to which the convention, as a body of men, was subject. They will also remember that they themselves are only men, and ought not assume infallibility in re-judging the fallible opinions of others.
With equal readiness it will be seen that, besides these inducements to candor, many allowances ought to be made for the difficulties inherent in the convention's task itself.

The novelty of the undertaking strikes us immediately. These papers have shown that the existing Confederation is founded on fallacious principles. Consequently, we must change this first foundation, along with the structure resting on it. They have shown that other confederacies which might serve as precedents have been corrupted by the same mistaken principles. They can therefore furnish only the light of warning beacons, signaling the course to be avoided, without showing the one to follow. The most the convention could do in such a situation was to avoid the errors suggested by past experience of other countries and our own, and to provide a convenient way of correcting their own errors as future experience reveals them.

Among the difficulties facing the convention, a major one was combining the necessary stability and energy of government with the inviolable attention due to liberty and the republican form. Without substantially accomplishing this, they would have very imperfectly fulfilled the object of their appointment or the public's expectations. Yet that this could not easily be accomplished will be denied by no one unwilling to betray his ignorance of the subject. Energy in government is essential to security against external and internal danger, and to the prompt and salutary execution of laws which form the very definition of good government. Stability is essential to national character and to the advantages tied to it, as well as to that repose and confidence in the people's minds which are among the chief blessings of civil society. Irregular and changeable legislation is not only an evil in itself; it is hated by the people. We may pronounce with assurance that the people of this country, enlightened as they are about the nature and effects of good government, will never be satisfied until some remedy is applied to the vicissitudes and uncertainties characterizing state administrations. But on comparing these valuable ingredients with the vital principles of liberty, we see at once the difficulty of mixing them in their proper proportions. The genius of republican liberty seems to demand on one side that all power be derived from the people, and that those entrusted with it remain dependent on the people through short terms of office. Even within those short periods, trust should be placed not in a few hands but in many. Stability, on the contrary, requires that those holding power continue in office for a long time. Frequent change of men results from frequent elections, and frequent change of measures from frequent change of men. Meanwhile, energy in government requires not only some duration of power but also its execution by a single hand.
How far the convention may have succeeded in this part of their work will appear better on closer view. From the brief survey here taken, it must be clear that this was an arduous task.

No less arduous must have been the task of marking the proper line between the authority of the general government and that of the states. Every man will recognize this difficulty as he is accustomed to contemplating extensive and complicated subjects. The faculties of the mind itself have never yet been distinguished and defined with satisfactory precision, despite the efforts of the most acute philosophers. Sense, perception, judgment, desire, will, memory, imagination are separated by such delicate shades and minute gradations that their boundaries have eluded the most subtle investigation, remaining a fertile source of ingenious controversy. The boundaries between the great kingdoms of nature, and even more between their various provinces and lesser portions, illustrate the same truth. The most diligent naturalists have never succeeded in tracing with certainty the line separating vegetable life from unorganized matter, or marking the end of the former and the start of the animal empire. A still greater obscurity lies in the distinctive characters by which objects in each of these great departments of nature have been arranged.

When we pass from the works of nature, in which all delineations are perfectly accurate (and appear otherwise only from the imperfection of our eyes), to the institutions of man, in which the obscurity arises both from the object and from the organ contemplating it, we must moderate our expectations of human sagacity still further. Experience has taught us that no skill in the science of government has been able to define with sufficient certainty its three great provinces — legislative, executive, and judiciary — or even the privileges and powers of different legislative branches. Questions arise daily in practice that prove the obscurity reigning in these subjects, puzzling the greatest experts in political science.

The experience of ages, with the combined labors of the most enlightened legislators and jurists, has been equally unsuccessful in defining the objects and limits of different bodies of law and tribunals of justice. The precise extent of common law, statute law, maritime law, ecclesiastical law, the law of corporations, and other local laws and customs remains to be clearly settled in Great Britain, where accuracy in such matters has been pursued more diligently than anywhere else. The jurisdiction of her several courts — general and local, of law, equity, admiralty, and so on — is a source of frequent and intricate dispute, sufficiently indicating the indeterminate limits by which they are circumscribed. All new laws, however skillfully drafted and however maturely deliberated, are considered more or less obscure and equivocal until their meaning is settled by a series of particular decisions and adjudications. Besides the obscurity arising from complex objects and imperfect human faculties, the medium through which our conceptions are conveyed adds further difficulty. The use of words is to express ideas. Clarity therefore requires not only that ideas be distinctly formed but that they be expressed by words distinctly and exclusively appropriate to them. But no language is rich enough to supply words for every complex idea, or accurate enough to avoid words that equivocally denote different ideas. So however accurately objects may be discriminated in themselves, the definition of them may be rendered inaccurate by the inaccuracy of the terms used. This unavoidable inaccuracy must be greater according to the complexity and novelty of the objects defined. When the Almighty himself condescends to address mankind in their own language, his meaning, however luminous, is rendered dim and doubtful by the cloudy medium through which it is conveyed.

Here, then, are three sources of vague and incorrect definitions: indistinctness of the object, imperfection of the organ of conception, and inadequacy of the vehicle of ideas. Any one of these must produce some degree of obscurity. The convention, in marking the boundary between federal and state jurisdictions, must have experienced the full effect of all three.

To the difficulties already mentioned must be added the conflicting claims of larger and smaller states. We cannot err in supposing that the larger would contend for participation in government fully proportioned to their superior wealth and importance, and that the smaller would be no less tenacious of the equality they currently enjoy. We may well suppose that neither side would entirely yield to the other, and consequently that the struggle could end only by compromise. It is also extremely probable that, after the ratio of representation was adjusted, this very compromise must have produced a fresh struggle between the same parties to give such a turn to the organization of government, and to the distribution of its powers, as would increase the importance of the branches in which they had respectively obtained the greatest share of influence. There are features in the Constitution that warrant each of these suppositions. Insofar as either is well founded, it shows the convention must have been compelled to sacrifice theoretical propriety to the force of extraneous considerations.

Nor would large and small states alone have lined up against each other on various points. Other combinations, resulting from differences of local position and policy, must have created additional difficulties. As every state may be divided into different districts, and its citizens into different classes giving rise to contending interests and local jealousies, so the different parts of the United States are distinguished from each other by a variety of circumstances producing a like effect on a larger scale. And although this variety of interests, for reasons sufficiently explained in a former paper, may have a beneficial influence on the administration of the government once formed, everyone must be sensible of the contrary influence experienced in the task of forming it.

Would it be surprising if, under the pressure of all these difficulties, the convention had been forced into some deviations from that artificial structure and regular symmetry which an abstract view of the subject might lead an ingenious theorist to bestow on a Constitution planned in his study or imagination? The real wonder is that so many difficulties were surmounted, and surmounted with a unanimity almost as unprecedented as it must have been unexpected. It is impossible for any candid man to reflect on this without sharing the astonishment. It is impossible for the man of pious reflection not to perceive in it a finger of that Almighty hand which has been so frequently and signally extended to our relief in the critical stages of the revolution.

We had occasion in a former paper to note the repeated unsuccessful attempts in the United Netherlands to reform the baneful and notorious vices of their constitution. The history of nearly all the great councils held among mankind to reconcile their discordant opinions, calm their mutual jealousies, and adjust their respective interests is a history of factions, contentions, and disappointments. It may be classed among the darkest pictures displaying the infirmities and depravities of the human character. If a few scattered instances present a brighter aspect, they serve only as exceptions to admonish us of the general truth, and by their luster to darken the gloom of the contrasting prospect. In tracing the causes of these exceptions and applying them to the case before us, we are led to two important conclusions. First, the convention must have enjoyed, in a very singular degree, an exemption from the pestilent influence of party animosities — the disease most common to deliberative bodies and most apt to contaminate their proceedings. Second, all the deputations composing the convention were either satisfied by the final act, or were induced to accede to it by deep conviction of the necessity of sacrificing private opinions and partial interests to the public good, and by despair of seeing this necessity diminished by delays or new experiments.
